title: Common Mistakes That Weaken an RTI Application
excerpt: Many RTI applications get vague answers or are returned for avoidable reasons. Here are the most common mistakes and how to avoid them.
content_html:
The RTI Act is simple to use, but small mistakes can lead to vague replies, long delays or outright refusals. Most of them are easy to avoid once you know what to look for.

1. Asking "why" instead of "what"

The Act gives a right to information that exists in records. A PIO is not required to explain decisions or give opinions. "Why was this permit issued?" may get a one-line reply. "Copy of the file notings and approval order for this permit" will get the actual documents.

2. Being vague

"All information about the lake" is too broad. The PIO may reply that the request is unclear. Name the water body precisely, give a time period and list the specific documents you want.

3. Sending it to the wrong office

Applications sent to the wrong authority must be transferred, but that adds delay. Spend a few minutes working out which office actually holds the records.

4. Packing too much into one application

Long, multi-subject applications are harder to answer and easier to partially ignore. Split them by subject and by authority.

5. Not keeping proof of filing

Every deadline, for the reply and for appeals, runs from the date the application was received. Without a postal receipt or dated acknowledgement, you cannot prove when the clock started.

6. Missing appeal deadlines

The first appeal must normally be filed within 30 days, and the second within 90 days of the first appeal's decision. Note these dates as soon as you file.

An RTI is a paper trail. Every gap in your records is a gap the other side can use.

7. Ignoring the fee details

Fees and accepted payment methods differ between central and state authorities. An application with the wrong fee, or no fee, can be returned. Check your state's rules before sending.

8. Writing an angry letter

It is natural to be frustrated about a damaged lake or a dumping site, but accusations and emotional language don't help an RTI application. Keep it neutral and factual. Save the argument for complaints, appeals and public campaigns, where the documents you get from RTI will make it much stronger.

A quick checklist

  • Right public authority and PIO address.
  • Clear, numbered questions asking for records.
  • Specific place and time period.
  • Correct fee, or proof of exemption.
  • Copy kept, proof of sending kept.
  • Reply and appeal deadlines noted.

cover_caption: Most weak RTI replies trace back to how the questions were asked.

title: Plant Native, Not Ornamental: A Guide for Housing Societies
excerpt: Many housing society gardens are full of imported ornamental plants that local birds and insects cannot use. Choosing native trees makes green spaces work for nature too.
content_html:
Walk through many apartment compounds and you will see neat lawns, clipped hedges and imported ornamental palms. They look tidy, but they often do little for local birds, butterflies and bees. Choosing native plants can turn the same space into a small habitat.

What "native" means

A native plant is one that grows naturally in your region and has evolved alongside its insects, birds and soil. Local wildlife knows how to use it: for nectar, fruit, nesting or shelter.

Why native plants are better

  • They feed wildlife. Local insects feed on native leaves and flowers, and birds feed on those insects and on native fruit.
  • They suit the climate. Once established, they usually need less watering and care.
  • They are less likely to become invasive. Some imported ornamentals spread aggressively and crowd out local plants.

Some widely used native trees

Trees native to India that are commonly planted include neem, jamun, mango, banyan and peepal. Large figs like banyan and peepal need a lot of space and should be planted away from buildings and pipes. Your local forest department, a botanical garden or an experienced naturalist can suggest species that suit your specific area and soil.

Ask not only whether a plant will look good, but whether anything else will be able to live on it.

Planning a native planting

  1. Survey the space: note sunlight, soil, drainage and nearby structures.
  2. Mix layers: combine trees, shrubs and ground cover, not just a row of trees.
  3. Leave some areas wild: a patch of leaf litter or uncut grass helps insects.
  4. Plant at the right time: the start of the monsoon gives saplings the best chance.
  5. Plan for aftercare: saplings need watering and protection for at least their first couple of years.

Getting the society on board

Start with a small corner rather than the whole compound. Invite residents, especially children, to help plant and care for it. Once people see birds and butterflies arrive, it becomes much easier to convince the committee to do more.

cover_caption: Native trees support far more local wildlife than imported ornamentals.

title: World Wetlands Day: Why February 2 Matters
excerpt: World Wetlands Day marks the date in 1971 when the Ramsar Convention was signed. Here is the story behind the day, the Ramsar Sites in Maharashtra, and how to use the day locally.
content_html:
Every year on 2 February, people around the world mark World Wetlands Day. The date is not random. It recalls the signing of an international treaty that remains the main global agreement on wetlands.

The Ramsar Convention

On 2 February 1971, governments met in the Iranian city of Ramsar and adopted the Convention on Wetlands, usually called the Ramsar Convention. It is one of the oldest international environmental agreements. Countries that join it commit to the wise use of their wetlands and to designating important wetlands as "Wetlands of International Importance", widely known as Ramsar Sites.

India and Ramsar

India is a party to the convention and has designated many Ramsar Sites across the country, a list that has grown considerably in recent years. Maharashtra's Ramsar Sites include Nandur Madhmeshwar in Nashik district, Lonar Lake in Buldhana district, and Thane Creek, right on the edge of Mumbai, where flocks of flamingos gather in the shallow mudflats.

Being a Ramsar Site brings international recognition and attention, but it does not by itself stop pollution, encroachment or overuse. Day-to-day protection still depends on national and state laws, and on local people.

How the day became global

World Wetlands Day has been observed since the late 1990s. In 2021, the United Nations General Assembly recognised it as an official UN international day, giving it a wider platform.

One day a year will not save a wetland. But it can be the day someone notices the one down the road.

Ideas for marking the day locally

  • Visit a nearby wetland with family, students or neighbours, and simply observe.
  • Organise a bird walk with someone who knows local species.
  • Hold a talk at a school about what wetlands do.
  • Map local water bodies and compare them with older maps to see what has been lost.
  • Write to your local body asking how a nearby wetland is being protected.

Beyond one day

The most useful thing about World Wetlands Day is the attention it creates. Use that attention to start something that lasts: a regular monitoring walk, a residents' group, or a steady habit of asking questions about the water bodies around you.

title: Devrais: The Sacred Groves of Maharashtra
excerpt: Across the Sahyadris and the Konkan, village communities have protected small patches of forest called devrais for generations. They hold rare plants, feed water sources and are under quiet pressure.
content_html:
In many villages across the Sahyadri hills and the Konkan coast, there is a patch of old, dense forest that nobody cuts. It is known as a devrai, a sacred grove dedicated to a local deity. Similar groves exist across India under different names, such as kavu in Kerala and orans in Rajasthan.

Forests protected by belief

Most devrais were never protected by law. They survived because communities agreed, often through generations of custom, not to fell trees, collect timber or disturb the ground there. Dead wood and fallen leaves are left where they lie. That shared restraint has kept some groves in remarkably natural condition.

Why they matter for nature

Living seed banks

Because they have been left alone for so long, devrais can hold large old trees, climbers, shrubs and medicinal plants that have become rare in the surrounding landscape of farms, plantations and settlements.

Water sources

Many groves sit near springs, streams or ponds. Thick leaf litter and undisturbed soil help monsoon rain soak into the ground, which can keep nearby water sources flowing longer into the dry season.

Shelter for wildlife

Birds, bats, reptiles, insects and small mammals use groves as refuges in landscapes that are otherwise cleared or built up.

The pressures they face

  • Land disputes and changing ownership, where the grove ends up on a plot someone wants to use.
  • Clearing parts of a grove to build larger concrete temples, halls or compound walls.
  • Weakening of the customs that once protected them.
  • Roads, quarries and construction pushing up against grove edges.
  • Invasive plants and dumping at the margins.
A sacred grove is a reminder that conservation existed long before the word did.

Keeping groves alive

The groves that survive best are the ones whose communities still value them. The simplest help is often to leave a grove as it is: no clearing, no burning of leaf litter, no concrete inside it. Recording the plants and animals found there, with the community's permission, builds a picture of what each grove holds and why it is worth keeping. When a new road or building is planned nearby, asking early how it will affect the grove is far easier than trying to undo damage later.

cover_caption: Sacred groves often hold plants that have vanished from the surrounding land.

title: How to Document an Environmental Problem So It Gets Taken Seriously
excerpt: A vague complaint is easy to ignore. Dated photographs, precise locations and a simple log make a much stronger case. A practical guide for residents.
content_html:
When people see dumping, filling or pollution, their first complaint is often a phone call or a message that says, roughly, "someone is ruining the lake." That kind of complaint is easy to ignore. Clear, organised evidence is much harder to brush aside.

Record the basics every time

For each incident, note:

  • Date and time.
  • Exact location: a landmark, survey number if known, and map coordinates from your phone.
  • What you saw: dumping, filling, a pipe discharging, trees being cut.
  • Vehicles involved: type and registration number, if visible and safe to note.

Taking useful photographs

  1. Wide shot first: show the surroundings so the place can be identified.
  2. Then the detail: the debris, the pipe, the damage.
  3. Same spot, over time: photograph the same view weekly or monthly to show change.
  4. Keep originals: do not edit or crop the original files. Keep a copy with its metadata intact.
One photograph shows a moment. Twenty photographs of the same place over a year show a pattern.

Keep a simple log

A spreadsheet or notebook with one line per incident is enough: date, location, what happened, photo file names, and whom you reported it to. Over time, this log becomes the backbone of any complaint, RTI application or legal case.

Stay safe

  • Do not confront people doing the dumping or filling.
  • Photograph from a public place, at a safe distance.
  • If you feel threatened, leave and report it later.
  • Consider documenting in pairs.

Making the complaint

Send a written complaint to the right authority: your local body, the village or revenue office, or the pollution control board, depending on the problem. Attach your best photographs and a summary of your log. Keep a copy, and note the date you sent it. If there is no response within a reasonable time, the Right to Information Act can help you find out what action, if any, was taken.

cover_caption: Good evidence records what happened, where and when.

title: Monsoon Flooding in Our Towns: Why Drains Are Only Part of the Story
excerpt: Every monsoon brings waterlogged roads and flooded homes. Bigger drains help, but the deeper causes are the loss of land that used to absorb and hold rain.
content_html:
Every monsoon, the same pictures appear: roads turned into rivers, vehicles stalled in knee-deep water, homes flooded at the ground floor. The usual response is a call to clean and widen drains. That matters, but it is only part of the story.

Where rain used to go

Before towns grew dense, rain had several places to go:

  • It soaked into open soil, gardens and paddy fields.
  • It collected in ponds, tanks, lakes and marshes.
  • It flowed along natural streams and channels to rivers and the sea.

As these spaces are paved, filled or built over, the same rain falls on hard surfaces and runs off all at once. Drains designed for a different town are suddenly asked to carry far more water, far faster.

Common causes of urban flooding

Lost water bodies

Ponds and low-lying marshes that once stored floodwater have been filled in. The rain that used to fill them now fills streets instead.

Blocked natural channels

Small streams that once carried water away are narrowed, covered or built over, creating bottlenecks.

Paved surfaces

Concrete yards, roads and parking lots stop water from soaking in.

Solid waste in drains

Plastic and debris clog drains just when they are needed most.

Water always finds the lowest point. Planning decides whether that point is a pond or someone's living room.

What helps

  1. Protect remaining water bodies and their seasonal flood zones.
  2. Keep natural channels open and avoid building on them.
  3. Let water soak in with permeable paving, unpaved yards and recharge pits.
  4. Harvest rainwater from rooftops to reduce runoff.
  5. Keep waste out of drains through proper segregation and collection.

What residents can do

Notice where water collects in your area and where it used to drain before. Ask your local body about plans for nearby ponds and channels. Before buying or building, check whether the land was once low-lying or wet. These questions are much easier to ask before the monsoon than in the middle of it.

cover_caption: Waterlogging is often a land-use problem as much as a drainage problem.

title: Writing RTI Questions About a Local Water Body
excerpt: If a lake or pond near you is shrinking or being polluted, an RTI application can uncover records about it. Here are sample questions and how to frame them.
content_html:
When residents notice a lake being filled or polluted, they often don't know who is responsible or what official records exist. An RTI application can help find out. The key is asking clear questions that point to specific documents.

Start with the basics

Before writing, gather what you already know: the water body's local name, the village or ward, any survey numbers, and the nearest landmark. The more precisely you identify it, the less room there is for a vague reply.

Questions about ownership and boundaries

  • Copy of land records showing the survey number(s), extent and classification of the water body.
  • Copy of any survey or map showing its official boundary.
  • Name of the department responsible for maintaining it.

Questions about construction and permissions

  • Copies of any building permits or land-use changes issued for plots adjoining the water body during a stated period.
  • Copies of any orders permitting filling, conversion or reclassification of any part of it.

Questions about complaints and action taken

  • Copies of complaints received about dumping, filling or pollution at the water body during a stated period.
  • Copies of inspection reports, notices issued and action taken on those complaints.

Questions about pollution

  • Copies of any water quality test reports for the water body.
  • List of any outlets, drains or establishments known to discharge into it, and any consents issued.
"Copy of the inspection report dated…" will get a document. "Why has nothing been done?" will usually get a sentence.

Framing tips

  1. Ask for copies of records, not explanations or opinions.
  2. Give a time period, such as "from 1 January 2020 to date".
  3. Split by authority: send land questions to the revenue office and pollution questions to the pollution control board, rather than one long list to one office.
  4. Keep the list short: five to eight clear questions usually work better than twenty.
  5. Ask for inspection of files if you are unsure exactly which documents exist.

After you receive the reply

Compare the official boundary with what you see on the ground today. Check dates on permissions against when filling began. The gaps between the record and reality are often what makes a complaint or legal petition possible.
cover_alt: Illustration of a lake at dusk under a purple and pink sky, with a low orange sun, dark hills and reeds along the right-hand shore.
cover_caption: Specific, document-based questions get the most useful answers.
meta_title: Writing RTI Questions About a Local Water Body

title: Urban Lakes Are Not Empty Land
excerpt: Lakes in our towns and cities are often filled, fenced or turned into sewage sinks. They are working infrastructure for flood control and groundwater, and should be protected as such.
content_html:
Many Indian towns grew around their lakes and tanks. These water bodies collected monsoon rain, fed wells, and gave people a place to wash, fish and gather. As towns expanded, many of those lakes were filled in or slowly turned into drains.

Lakes are infrastructure

An urban lake is not decoration. It is part of how a city manages water:

  • Flood storage: during heavy rain, lakes take in runoff that would otherwise flood roads and homes.
  • Groundwater recharge: water seeping from the lake bed refills the aquifer under the neighbourhood.
  • Cooling: open water and the vegetation around it lower local temperatures.
  • Habitat: even small city lakes support birds, fish, frogs and insects.

How lakes are lost

Encroachment

Lake edges are often filled bit by bit, first with debris and then with buildings. Over time the lake shrinks without any single decision ever being made to remove it.

Cut-off inflow channels

Lakes are fed by small streams and channels. When these are blocked or built over, the lake starves and dries out, which makes it easier to claim as land.

Sewage

Untreated sewage turns a lake into a foul-smelling pond. Once residents see it as a nuisance, filling it in starts to look like a solution.

When a lake is filled, the rain that used to fall into it still arrives every monsoon. It just ends up somewhere else.

What good lake protection looks like

  1. The lake's full boundary, including its seasonal high-water area, is surveyed and recorded.
  2. Inflow and outflow channels are kept open.
  3. Sewage is diverted and treated before it reaches the lake.
  4. A buffer zone around the lake stays free of construction.
  5. Residents can see who is responsible for the lake and how to raise problems.

Start with your own neighbourhood

Find out whether there is a lake, tank or pond near you, and who owns and manages it. Old maps and land records can show how large it used to be. If you see dumping or construction at the edge, document it and report it. Lakes rarely have a loud constituency, so every resident who pays attention matters.

cover_caption: City lakes are part of the drainage system, not spare land waiting for a use.

title: Start a Neighbourhood Composting Group
excerpt: Wet kitchen waste is one of the biggest reasons dumps smell, burn and leak. A small composting group can turn it into useful soil. Here is how to start one.
content_html:
Wet kitchen waste, from vegetable peels to tea leaves and leftover food, makes up a large share of household rubbish. When it is mixed with plastic and sent to a dump, it rots, smells, attracts animals and leaks dirty water into the ground. When it is composted, it becomes soil.

Why do it as a group

Many people try composting alone and give up after a smelly first attempt. A neighbourhood group helps because:

  • Members share bins, tools and space.
  • Experienced members help newcomers fix problems.
  • A shared site can handle more waste and produce more compost.
  • It is easier to keep going when others are doing it too.

Getting started

1. Find five or six households

Start small. A handful of committed homes is better than fifty who drop out after a month.

2. Choose a method

  • Home bins or pots: good for individual flats.
  • Shared aerobic bins: good for a building or a lane.
  • Pit composting: works where there is open ground.

3. Agree what goes in

Vegetable and fruit scraps, tea leaves, coffee grounds, eggshells and dry leaves are all suitable. Keep out plastic, glass, metal and medicines. Some groups also avoid large amounts of cooked food, meat and oil, which can attract animals and slow things down.

The basic recipe

Compost needs a balance of wet "greens" (kitchen scraps) and dry "browns" (dry leaves, shredded cardboard, sawdust). A common rule of thumb is to add roughly two to three parts brown for every part green, by volume.

If it smells, add browns. If nothing is happening, add greens and a little water.

Common problems

  • Bad smell: too wet or too many greens. Add dry material and mix.
  • Flies: cover fresh scraps with a layer of browns.
  • Nothing breaking down: too dry, or not enough greens. Add water and fresh scraps.

Using the compost

Finished compost is dark, crumbly and smells like earth. Use it for pots, kitchen gardens, community plantings or street trees. Sharing the first harvest with the group is a good way to keep everyone motivated.
cover_alt: Illustration of layers of dark soil topped with scattered green and brown leaves, with a young seedling growing from the top layer.
cover_caption: Kitchen waste can become soil instead of a problem.

title: India's Single-Use Plastic Ban: What Changed and What Didn't
excerpt: Since July 2022, many single-use plastic items have been banned in India. Here is what the ban covers, what it leaves out, and why enforcement still depends on all of us.
content_html:
From 1 July 2022, India banned the manufacture, import, stocking, distribution, sale and use of a list of single-use plastic items. The change came through amendments to the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016. More than four years on, it is worth looking at what the ban actually covers.

What is banned

The list focuses on small, low-value items that are hard to collect and recycle. It includes:

  • Earbuds with plastic sticks, and plastic sticks for balloons, candy, ice cream and flags.
  • Polystyrene (thermocol) for decoration.
  • Plastic plates, cups, glasses and cutlery such as forks, spoons and knives.
  • Straws, trays and stirrers.
  • Wrapping or packing films around sweet boxes, invitation cards and cigarette packets.
  • Plastic or PVC banners below a set thickness.

Plastic carry bags were also tightened in stages, with the minimum thickness raised to 120 microns from 31 December 2022.

What the ban does not cover

Many of the plastics we see most often are not on the list:

  • Multi-layered packaging for snacks, biscuits and shampoo sachets.
  • Most PET bottles for water and soft drinks.
  • Thicker carry bags that meet the thickness standard.

For packaging, the rules rely on Extended Producer Responsibility: brand owners and producers are expected to take responsibility for collecting and processing the plastic they put into the market.

A ban removes some items from the shelf. It does not remove the habit that put them there.

Why enforcement varies

Enforcement falls largely on state pollution control boards and local bodies, and it differs a great deal from place to place. Banned items still turn up in markets and at events, often because cheaper alternatives are not easily available to small vendors.

What you can do

  1. Carry your own bag, bottle and, where practical, cutlery.
  2. Choose vendors who use alternatives, and tell them why.
  3. Ask event organisers, including at weddings and festivals, to avoid banned items.
  4. Report persistent sale of banned items to your local body.
  5. Separate dry waste so that recyclable plastic actually reaches recyclers.

Rules change over time. Check the latest notification from the environment ministry or your state pollution control board for current details.

cover_caption: Banned items are only part of the plastic problem on our beaches.

title: Mangroves: The Coastal Guardians We Keep Losing
excerpt: Mangroves protect coastlines, shelter young fish and store large amounts of carbon. Here is why these salt-tolerant forests deserve far more protection than they get.
content_html:
Mangroves are trees and shrubs that have learned to live where few plants can: in salty, muddy water that rises and falls with the tide. Along estuaries and backwaters they form dense green walls that are easy to overlook, and easy to clear.

How mangroves survive

Many mangrove species grow arching prop roots that hold them steady in soft mud. Others send up pencil-like breathing roots through the waterlogged soil. Some filter salt at the roots, while others push excess salt out through their leaves.

Why they matter

Natural sea walls

The tangle of roots slows down waves and tidal surges and holds the shoreline together. Coasts with healthy mangrove belts generally suffer less erosion than coasts where they have been removed.

Fish nurseries

The calm, sheltered water between the roots is where many fish, prawns and crabs spend their early lives. Coastal fishing communities depend on this, often without realising how closely.

Carbon stores

Mangrove soils hold a large amount of carbon, built up over long periods. When mangroves are cut and the soil is disturbed, much of that carbon can be released.

What threatens them

  • Clearing for aquaculture ponds, ports and real estate.
  • Reclamation of tidal land by dumping earth and debris.
  • Plastic and solid waste caught in the roots.
  • Blocked tidal flow from poorly planned bunds and roads.
A mangrove does not need to be planted to be useful. The most valuable mangroves are the ones that are simply left alone.

Planting is not always the answer

Mangrove planting drives are popular, but survival rates depend heavily on choosing the right species for the right spot and restoring tidal water flow. Protecting existing mangroves is almost always cheaper and more effective than replacing lost ones.

What residents can do

Report dumping and filling in tidal areas. Avoid buying property built on reclaimed mangrove land. If you join a planting event, ask whether the organisers have checked the site's tides, soil and species, and who will look after the saplings afterwards.

cover_caption: Mangrove roots slow waves and trap sediment along the shoreline.

title: RTI First and Second Appeals: What to Do When You Get No Reply
excerpt: A missing or incomplete RTI reply is not the end of the road. The Act gives you a first appeal and a second appeal. Here is how each one works.
content_html:
Many RTI applications get a full answer on the first try. Many don't. Some get no reply at all, some get a partial one, and some are refused with a reason you disagree with. The RTI Act, 2005 builds in two levels of appeal for exactly these situations.

When you can appeal

  • You received no reply within the time limit (normally 30 days).
  • The information was refused, and you disagree with the reason.
  • The information given was incomplete, misleading or not what you asked for.
  • You were asked to pay a fee you think is unreasonable.

The first appeal

The first appeal goes to the First Appellate Authority, an officer senior to the PIO in the same public authority. The PIO's reply should name this officer. If it doesn't, address the appeal to the head of the office.

  • Deadline: within 30 days of receiving the reply, or of the date the reply was due.
  • Content: your details, a copy of the original application and any reply, and a short explanation of what is missing or wrong.
  • Response: the appellate authority should normally decide within 30 days, extendable to 45 days with reasons.

The second appeal

If the first appeal fails, you can go to the Information Commission: the Central Information Commission for central authorities, or your State Information Commission for state and local authorities.

  • Deadline: within 90 days from the date the first appeal decision was made or should have been made.
  • Content: copies of the original application, the PIO's reply, the first appeal and its decision, with a clear statement of what you are asking the Commission to order.
Each stage builds on the paper trail of the last. Keep copies of everything, in order.

What the Commission can do

An Information Commission can order the information to be provided. If a PIO refused without reasonable cause, delayed without reason or gave false information, the Commission can also impose a penalty on that officer, calculated per day of delay up to a maximum limit set in the Act.

Practical tips

  1. Write appeals calmly and factually. Point to the specific questions that were not answered.
  2. Number your attachments and refer to them in the text.
  3. Keep postal receipts and acknowledgements.
  4. Be patient: second appeals can take a long time to be heard.

This is a general guide, not legal advice. Check your state's rules for any specific procedure or format.
cover_alt: Illustration of layered paper documents with a green heading bar, a round stamp mark and a dark pen resting beside them.
cover_caption: Appeals have their own deadlines, so keep proof of every date.

title: The Wetlands Rules, 2017: What They Mean for Your Local Water Body
excerpt: A plain-language look at the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017: who is responsible for wetlands, what is prohibited, and where the gaps are.
content_html:
India's main national rules for protecting wetlands are the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, issued by the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. They replaced an earlier set of rules from 2010. Here is what residents should know about them.

Who is responsible

The rules give much of the responsibility to the states. Each state and union territory is expected to set up a State Wetlands Authority, which identifies wetlands, recommends them for notification and plans how they should be managed.

What the rules prohibit

Inside a wetland that has been formally notified, the rules list activities that are not allowed. These include:

  • Converting the wetland for non-wetland uses, including encroachment.
  • Setting up or expanding industries.
  • Dumping solid waste.
  • Discharging untreated waste and effluents.
  • Building permanent structures close to the wetland, with limited exceptions such as boat jetties.
  • Poaching.

The catch: notification

These protections apply most clearly to wetlands that have been officially identified and notified. Many lakes, ponds and marshes, especially smaller ones, have never been through that process. That leaves them in a weaker legal position, even when they are ecologically important.

A rule only protects a wetland that the system has formally recognised. Recognition is often the first battle.

How this connects to other laws

Wetlands can also be covered by other rules: coastal regulation for tidal and backwater areas, water pollution law for discharges, and state laws on paddy land and wetland conversion. A single water body may fall under several of these at once, which is part of why enforcement can be confusing.

What residents can do

  1. Find out whether the water body near you has been identified or notified as a wetland.
  2. If it has, ask the relevant authority for its boundary and management plan.
  3. If it hasn't, ask what steps would be needed to have it assessed.
  4. Use the Right to Information Act for documents you cannot get informally.

Rules on paper matter, but they work best when local people know they exist and ask for them to be applied.

This post is a general explainer, not legal advice. For a specific case, check the current text of the rules and consult someone with legal expertise.

title: How to Organise a Lake Clean-Up That Actually Helps
excerpt: Clean-up drives are popular, but many end with waste piled at the roadside. A practical guide to planning a clean-up that leaves a water body genuinely better off.
content_html:
Clean-up drives bring people together and make a visible difference in a single morning. But a badly planned one can do more harm than good: waste bags left at the roadside, birds disturbed in nesting season, or volunteers hurt by broken glass. Here is how to plan one properly.

Before the day

Get permission

Find out who manages the water body, whether a local body, a temple trust, an irrigation department or a private owner, and inform them in writing. Ask whether they can help with waste collection.

Arrange disposal first

This is the step most often skipped. Before you announce the event, confirm who will collect the waste and where it will go. Without this, the clean-up just moves rubbish from the water to the roadside.

Check the timing

Avoid nesting seasons and heavy rain. Early mornings are cooler and better for volunteers.

Plan for safety

  • Gloves for everyone, and sturdy footwear.
  • No one goes into deep water.
  • Sharp objects and medical waste are flagged, not picked up by hand.
  • Drinking water and a basic first-aid kit on site.

On the day

  1. Start with a short briefing on safety and what not to touch.
  2. Split volunteers into small teams with clear zones.
  3. Separate waste as you collect it: plastics, glass, cloth and other materials.
  4. Leave natural material such as fallen leaves and branches in place. It is part of the habitat.
  5. Count or weigh what you collect, and photograph it.
The most useful data from a clean-up is not how much was collected, but what it was and where it came from.

After the day

Look at what you found. If most of the waste is from one source, such as a nearby market, a drain outlet or a dumping spot, that is where the real work begins. Share your findings with the local body and ask what will stop the waste coming back.

Make it a habit

A single clean-up treats the symptom. Regular visits, combined with steady pressure on the sources of waste, are what change a water body over time. Consider a monthly or quarterly schedule with a small, committed group rather than one large event a year.

title: Why Wetlands Matter More Than Most People Think
excerpt: Marshes, backwaters and paddy-lake systems are often treated as wasteland. In reality they store floodwater, clean water and support a huge range of life.
content_html:
Ask people to picture a valuable ecosystem and most will imagine a forest. Fewer will think of a marsh, a backwater or a seasonally flooded field. Yet wetlands do some of the most useful work any landscape can do, and they are disappearing faster than many other habitats because they are so easy to dismiss as empty land.

What counts as a wetland

A wetland is any area where water covers the soil, or sits just below the surface, for all or part of the year. That includes lakes and ponds, marshes, mangroves, estuaries, backwaters, river floodplains and even well-managed paddy fields. India also has many temple tanks and village ponds that function as small wetlands.

The work wetlands do

They hold floodwater

A wetland behaves like a sponge. During heavy rain it soaks up water and releases it slowly, lowering the peak of a flood downstream. When wetlands are filled in and built over, that water has nowhere to go except into streets and homes.

They clean water

Plants and microbes in wetlands trap sediment and break down many pollutants. Water leaving a healthy marsh is often cleaner than the water that entered it.

They recharge groundwater

Standing water seeps down into the ground and refills the aquifers that wells and borewells depend on. Lose the wetland and nearby wells often run dry sooner in summer.

They support life

Wetlands are breeding grounds for fish, nurseries for prawns and crabs, and resting stops for migratory birds. Many local fishing livelihoods depend directly on them.

Why they keep shrinking

  • Filling for housing, roads and commercial plots.
  • Dumping of solid waste and construction debris.
  • Untreated sewage and industrial discharge.
  • Invasive weeds that choke open water.
  • Changes to natural water flow from bunds, canals and drains.
A wetland rarely disappears in one dramatic act. It is usually lost one truckload of debris at a time.

What you can do

Learn which water bodies exist near your home, and notice when they change. Photograph dumping or filling with the date and location. Ask your local body what protection a wetland has, and use the Right to Information Act if the answer is unclear. Small, steady attention from residents is often what keeps a wetland alive.

title: How to File an RTI Application: A Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: The Right to Information Act, 2005 lets any citizen ask a public authority for information. This guide walks through writing, sending and following up on an RTI application.
content_html:
The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 gives every Indian citizen the right to request information from public authorities. For environmental issues it is one of the most useful tools available: it can show who approved a project, whether a pollution complaint was acted upon, or what a lake's official boundary is.

Step 1: Identify the right public authority

Work out which office holds the information. For a local water body, that might be the panchayat or municipality, the revenue department, the irrigation department or the pollution control board. Sending your application to the right office saves time, although the law requires an office that receives an application meant for another to transfer it.

Step 2: Write the application

Address it to the Public Information Officer (PIO) of that authority. The application can be in English, Hindi or the official language of the area. Include:

  • Your name and address for reply.
  • A clear list of the information you want, in numbered points.
  • The time period the information covers.
  • Whether you want copies, or to inspect the records.

You do not need to give a reason for asking.

Step 3: Pay the fee

For central government authorities the application fee is ₹10. States set their own fees, so check the rules for your state. Applicants below the poverty line are exempt from fees on producing proof. There may also be a small charge for photocopies.

Step 4: Send it and keep proof

Send the application by registered post or speed post, or hand it over in person and get a dated acknowledgement. Many central government authorities also accept applications online through the official RTI portal. Keep a copy of everything you send.

The proof of the date you filed is as important as the application itself. Every deadline counts from that day.

Step 5: Wait for the reply

The PIO must normally respond within 30 days of receiving the application. If the information concerns someone's life or liberty, the limit is 48 hours. If the application is transferred to another authority, the clock can run slightly longer.

Step 6: If there is no reply or a poor reply

No response within the time limit is treated as a refusal. You can then file a first appeal with the officer senior to the PIO, known as the First Appellate Authority. We cover appeals in detail in a separate guide.

Tips for a strong application

  1. Ask for documents, not opinions: "copy of the approval order" rather than "why was this approved?"
  2. Keep each question short and specific.
  3. Limit each application to one subject.
  4. Keep a log of every application, date, reply and appeal.

This is a general guide, not legal advice. Fees and procedures can differ between states.
